title: Seattle bans landlords from charging 'junk fees' like pet rent
text:
The Seattle City Council passed legislation Tuesday to ban pet rent and other charges that housing advocates often call "junk fees."

Under the legislation, Seattle landlords must disclose fees in advertising rent prices, and they can’t charge fees for things like mail and package delivery. The legislation also gives the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections subpoena power over landlords and the ability to investigate suspected violations of regulations on security deposits and move-in costs. The new regulations don't go into effect until July 1, 2027.

The legislation does not stop landlords from charging pet deposits or charging tenants for damages related to their pets.

Some people, including District 7 Councilmember Bob Kettle, reject the “junk fee” term as pejorative.

The bill passed the City Council almost unanimously: District 4 Councilmember Maritza Rivera recused herself from the vote because she owns a rental property. Kettle submitted an amendment to allow pet rent but cap it. His amendment failed, and Kettle voted in support of the legislations along with the other Council members, including sponsor Dionne Foster, who holds a citywide seat.

The legislation's passage is a win for Mayor Katie Wilson, who spoke frequently of hidden fees last year during her campaign and who sees banning hidden fees as a way to forward her housing affordability agenda.

It’s unclear how many Seattle renters are burdened by fees tacked onto their rent. An Urban Institute study of a small number of rental ledgers across three landlords in Denver last year found utility administration charges, fees for the maintenance of common areas, package delivery fees, and traditional utilities like water, gas, and sewer could add 10% to 30% to renters’ total monthly costs.

“ My wife and I pay almost $100 a month, between pet rent – my dog is unemployed, so we're covering it for her – amenity fees for things like use of the building access control system and charges for common area stuff," Northgate resident Wes Mills said during public comment. “And that's after we've managed multiple times to beat back the sneaky opt-out-but-only-if-you-notice fees for stuff like liability waivers.”

Another speaker said she’d been charged $75 a month for her cat, though she said the cat had never damaged her apartment or the building.

Speakers from animal welfare organizations such as Seattle Humane and the ASPCA also supported the legislation.

Opponents such as the Rental Housing Association of Washington, which represents small landlords, say that these regulations will fall on “mom-and-pop” rentals while corporate landlords have ways to get around them.

“If you want to use a service, you have to pay for it,” said Kevin Schilling, a lobbyist for the Rental Housing Association (who is also a Burien City Council member). “And if we just take away the fee for a service, what's going to happen is either the costs to offer that service are going to be baked into somewhere else or the service is not going to be allowed.”

Schilling asked the Seattle City Council to include scaled requirements for smaller landlords, but they did not.
